title: Wrap-Up Check
description: 20 questions drawn at random from a pool of 30 — about five minutes. No score pressure: this is a recap, not an exam.

intake.lead: The Wrap-Up Check is anonymous — no results are sent anywhere and your answers stay on this machine, so there is no score pressure and you can retake it as often as you like. Pressing start just begins the twenty questions. If you would like to ask us something or hear more about Pentaho products and services, use Contact Us in the sidebar.

questions.scenario: You are building a transformation that filters a sales file and writes the valid rows to a table, and you want to see which rows leave the filter before anything is written.
questions.prompt: How do you inspect those rows in PDI?
options: Select the filter step and preview it
Add logging code to the step and redeploy it
Export the stream to CSV and open it in a spreadsheet
Run the transformation, then query the target table
questions.explanation: Previewing the filter step shows the rows arriving there, at any point while you build, without writing anything. Adding logging code and redeploying changes the thing you are trying to observe. Running the transformation and querying the table only shows what reached the end, after it has been written. Exporting to CSV is a manual detour that still writes the data out before you can look at it.

questions.scenario: You add a Text file input step for a delimited supplier file you have never opened, and it needs each column's name, type and format before anything downstream can use it.
questions.prompt: What does the 'Get Fields' button do for you here?
options: Reads every column as a String for later conversion in SQL
Parses the file and proposes data stream names, types and formats
Copies the field list from the last file the step read
Loads a schema definition that the supplier must provide
questions.explanation: Get Fields samples the file and proposes each column's name, type and format, and the grid lets you fix anything it guessed wrong, so the step works on a file PDI has never seen. It does not need a schema definition from the supplier. It does not leave everything as String; it infers types. It does not copy an earlier file's fields; it reads this one.

questions.scenario: You need one enriched sales output from four files: daily sales in CSV, a customer master in JSON, a product catalogue and a region reference.
questions.prompt: What must happen to the four sources before PDI can combine them?
options: Nothing: each has its own input step and joins in flight
They must first be loaded into a staging database
Each source needs an entry in a schema registry first
The JSON must be converted to CSV so the formats match
questions.explanation: Each file is read by its own input step, and once read everything is rows, so lookups and joins work on the streams in flight. Loading them into a staging database first is unnecessary. Converting the JSON to CSV is unnecessary, because the format difference disappears at the input step. PDI needs no schema registry to read or join files.

questions.scenario: A customer moves from North to South in the source file, and the nightly load runs Dimension lookup/update against a Type 2 customer dimension.
questions.prompt: What does the dimension hold for that customer after the load?
options: Two rows: North with its validity closed, South open-ended
One row, with North overwritten by South
A new row for every customer in the reloaded file
One rejected row, because the key already exists
questions.explanation: Type 2 keeps history: Dimension lookup/update closes the old version's validity window and inserts a new, open-ended version, leaving unchanged customers alone. Overwriting North with South is Type 1 behaviour, which loses the history. The existing key is expected, not a violation; that is how the step finds the version to close. Unchanged customers get no new rows, however much of the file is reloaded.

questions.scenario: Three supplier feeds load through one metadata-injection template driven by a control file of filenames, delimiters and targets, and a fourth supplier is being onboarded.
questions.prompt: What is the least work needed to start loading the fourth feed?
options: Copy the template and edit its input step for the new file
Regenerate the template transformation from the driver job
Build a new transformation dedicated to the fourth feed
Add one row describing the new feed to the control file
questions.explanation: Metadata injection turns configuration into data, so a new feed is a new control-file row and no transformation is opened. Copying the template and editing it defeats the point of having one template. A dedicated transformation per feed is the pattern metadata injection replaces. The template is never regenerated; it stays as it is and is filled in at run time.

questions.scenario: Transformations built and tested in Pentaho Developer Edition on a laptop now need to run every night in production.
questions.prompt: What does moving to a production deployment add?
options: Scheduled, monitored execution on a server
A commercial licence for production use, with support
A new pipeline format, so each transformation is rebuilt
Clustered, scaled-out execution
Compilation of every transformation into Java code
questions.explanation: Scheduled, monitored execution on a server, clustered scale-out, and a commercial licence with support are what production adds around the same transformations. A new pipeline format is not needed: what was built in Developer Edition is real PDI and moves to production as it is. Nothing is compiled into Java; the engine runs the transformation definition directly.

questions.scenario: A nightly load routes rows that fail a business rule into a rejects file while the rest continue to the target table.
questions.prompt: What does this design achieve that stopping the load on the first bad row would not?
options: Bad rows are corrected automatically before loading
Validation becomes unnecessary, since nothing can fail
The transformation runs measurably faster
Good rows still load, and failures return as a file to fix
questions.explanation: Routing turns bad data into a decision rather than a crash: the load completes and the rejects are a file the source team can act on. Speed is not the point, and routing is not measurably faster. Nothing corrects the bad rows automatically; they are set aside for a person to fix. Validation is still happening, since the rule is what decides which branch a row takes.

questions.scenario: A transformation that reads, validates, enriches and loads a sales file from a local folder must now read the same file from an Amazon S3 bucket.
questions.prompt: What has to change in the transformation?
options: Only the input step, because downstream steps see the same rows
The file must be copied locally first, since PDI cannot read S3
The whole design, rebuilt as a job instead of a transformation
Every step, because a cloud source yields a different row format
questions.explanation: Only the input step changes: once rows are in the stream, validation, lookups and output neither know nor care where they came from. A cloud source does not produce a different row format. A job is for orchestration and is not needed to read from S3. PDI reads S3 and other cloud and VFS locations directly, so no local copy is needed.

questions.scenario: Production needs your working transformations run in order every night, retried on failure, with an alert when the source file has not arrived.
questions.prompt: What in PDI provides that sequencing, retrying and alerting?
options: A job (.kjb), scheduled and monitored on a server
Schedule settings saved inside each transformation
A cron script that calls each transformation in turn
A Filter rows step at the start of each transformation
questions.explanation: A job is PDI's orchestration layer: it routes on success and failure, retries, and notifies, and a server runs it on a schedule with logging and history. A cron script is outside PDI and would have to reimplement the retries and alerts. A transformation carries no schedule of its own. Filter rows routes rows inside a transformation; it cannot sequence or retry transformations.

questions.scenario: A consultant plans to use Pentaho Developer Edition (BSL 1.1) to evaluate PDI on a client's data, build a proof of concept, train the client's team and then run the client's nightly loads.
questions.prompt: Which part of that plan needs a commercial licence?
options: Building the proof of concept for the client
Training the client's team to build pipelines
Running the client's nightly loads in production
Evaluating PDI against the client's real data
questions.explanation: Running the pipelines in production is what needs a commercial licence, which also brings support and certified updates. Evaluating PDI against real data is covered by Developer Edition. Building a proof of concept is development, which is covered. Training the team is learning, which is covered. Developer Edition does not expire.

questions.scenario: A Filter rows step checks for a positive quantity, with one step after it writing valid orders to the warehouse and another writing to a review file.
questions.prompt: Where do the orders that fail the condition go?
options: Down the FALSE hop, to the step you assigned to it
Down the same hop as passing rows, flagged in a new field
Nowhere, because failing rows are discarded by default
Back to the input step, to be read again
questions.explanation: Filter rows has two real output hops, and the rows that fail go down the FALSE hop to whichever step you assigned it. They do not share a hop with the passing rows; TRUE and FALSE are separate streams. They are not discarded when a FALSE target is set. Rows never flow back to the input step.

questions.scenario: After you run Get Fields on a Text file input step, the Calculator after it already lists unit_price as a Number and order_date as a Date, before any data has been read.
questions.prompt: What is the Calculator using to know those types?
options: Types guessed again by the Calculator from the field names
A Java class that PDI generated to parse the file
A cached copy of the whole file, taken when Get Fields ran
Row metadata: each field's name, type and format
questions.explanation: Row metadata travels down the hops ahead of the data, so every downstream step knows each field's name, type and format at design time, which is also why a mis-typed field is caught before the run. Get Fields does not cache the file. PDI generates no Java class to parse it. The Calculator does not guess types from names; it is told them.

questions.scenario: A four-step transformation that reads a 20 GB file, filters it and writes two outputs completes on a server with 8 GB of RAM without running out of memory.
questions.prompt: How do the four steps execute to make that possible?
options: One after another, with each step finishing before the next starts
Only the input step runs; the rest apply as rows are written
In the order the steps were added to the canvas
All at once, each on its own thread, passing rows through small buffers
questions.explanation: Every step runs at once on its own thread, and only the rows in flight sit in the buffers between them, so the file never has to fit in memory. Running the steps one after another would require holding each step's full output. The order steps were added to the canvas has no bearing on execution. Every step runs, not only the input.

questions.scenario: A reviewer opening a pull request for a changed transformation (.ktr) can read, line by line, which step settings and hops changed.
questions.prompt: What makes that change readable in the diff?
options: A Git plugin shipped with PDI renders the binary .ktr as text
A .ktr file is XML describing the steps, their settings and the hops
PDI writes a readable summary file beside each compiled .ktr
The reviewer's IDE decodes the Java objects stored in the .ktr
questions.explanation: A .ktr is plain XML, and the engine executes that XML directly, so it diffs and merges like source code. There is no compiled .ktr with a summary written beside it. No plugin is needed, because the file is not binary. It holds no serialized Java objects, only an XML description of steps, settings and hops.

questions.scenario: You are enriching orders from a second source in which some orders match several rows, and orders with no match must still appear in the output.
questions.prompt: Which configuration combines the two streams correctly?
options: Database lookup, returning the first matching row
Stream lookup, keyed on the order id
Merge join, configured as an INNER join
Merge join, configured as a LEFT OUTER join
questions.explanation: Merge join returns every matching row, and LEFT OUTER keeps orders that have no match, which meets both requirements. An INNER join would drop the orders with no match. Stream lookup returns at most one match per row, so the extra matches would be lost. A Database lookup returning the first matching row also returns only one match per row.

questions.scenario: A Merge join on region_code, fed by two streams in the order their files were written, misses matches you know exist without logging any error.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: The join type is LEFT OUTER, which skips some matches
Neither input is sorted on region_code before the join
Merge join holds only a fixed number of keys in memory
The region file is read only after the sales file ends
questions.explanation: Merge join walks both streams in step, holding only the current row from each, so unsorted input silently passes over matches instead of raising an error; a Sort rows step on region_code before each input fixes it. LEFT OUTER keeps more rows, not fewer. Both files are read at the same time, not one after the other. Merge join streams its inputs rather than holding a fixed number of keys.

questions.scenario: Sales rows are joined to a regions file on region_code, and a region added to the sales system last week is not in the regions file yet.
questions.prompt: Why configure this join as LEFT OUTER rather than INNER?
options: So empty manager_email values are filled in automatically
So sales with an unknown region still reach the output
So the regions file is read before the sales file
So duplicate region rows do not multiply the sales rows
questions.explanation: An INNER join drops any sale whose region is missing from the regions file; LEFT OUTER keeps every sale and leaves the region fields empty, turning 'sales went missing' into 'a region needs adding'. The join type does not stop duplicate region rows multiplying sales; that needs unique keys. It does not change the order files are read. It fills nothing in; unmatched fields are left empty.

questions.scenario: A Calculator step multiplying unit_price, a Number, by quantity, an Integer, returns 100.0 as the line total for 2 × 49.99.
questions.prompt: What is causing the wrong total?
options: Quantity is in Field A, so the calculation runs as an Integer
Unit price is read as a String until it reaches Field B
The result field's precision is set to zero decimals
The Calculator rounds every result by default
questions.explanation: The Calculator works in Field A's data type, so an Integer in Field A rounds 49.99 to 50 before multiplying; putting unit_price in Field A keeps the pennies. A precision setting on the result would round the output, but 49.99 is already lost before the multiply. The Calculator does not round results by default. Unit price is already a Number from the input step; it is not a String.

questions.scenario: After the first Dimension lookup/update load of 20 distinct customers, the customer dimension holds 21 rows.
questions.prompt: Where did the extra row come from?
options: The step inserted an unknown member, key 0, for failed lookups
Pressing the SQL button inserted a test row
The source file's header row was loaded as a customer
One customer was loaded twice because of a duplicate id
questions.explanation: Dimension lookup/update inserts a technical unknown member with key 0 so that a fact row whose customer cannot be found is attached to it rather than dropped. No customer is duplicated; the source holds each one once. The header row is not loaded as data by the JSON or text input steps. The SQL button creates the table; it inserts no test rows.

questions.scenario: A driver job reads a control file listing three feeds, each with a different delimiter, and runs an injector transformation that fills a template through metadata injection.
questions.prompt: Why does the job run the injector once per control-file row rather than once for all three feeds?
options: A job cannot pass more than one row to a transformation
Each injection run fills the template with one configuration
Each feed must be sorted before it can be injected
The template can only read files smaller than 1 MB
questions.explanation: One injection run writes one set of values, one filename and one delimiter, into the template and executes that copy, so three configurations need three runs; executing for every input row supplies the loop. The template has no file-size limit. Jobs can pass many rows; running once per row is a choice made for injection. Feeds need no sorting to be injected.

questions.scenario: Three enrichment branches need to meet at one clearly named point before the output, and you want the canvas to stay readable.
questions.prompt: Which step gives you that junction without touching the data?
options: Filter rows, with a condition that is always true
Dummy, which performs no operation on the rows
Select values, passing the fields straight through
Blocking step, gathering the branches before release
questions.explanation: Dummy is a deliberate no-op: it changes nothing about the rows, so it serves purely as a named junction and a visual milestone. Select values does real work on fields, even when configured to pass them through. Filter rows evaluates a condition on every row. Blocking step changes when rows flow, holding them back, which is more than a junction should do.

questions.scenario: A Stream lookup adds the customer name to each sale by customer_id, and one sale carries a customer_id that is not in the customer master.
questions.prompt: What happens to that sale?
options: It is sent down the lookup step's error hop
It continues down the stream with the name left empty
The transformation stops on the unmatched key
It is dropped, because the lookup found no match
questions.explanation: Stream lookup enriches rather than filters: an unmatched key leaves the retrieved fields empty and the row carries on, which is why you check for empty values downstream when a missing reference matters. It is not dropped; that is what an inner join would do. The transformation does not stop. An unmatched key is not an error, so nothing goes to the error hop.

questions.scenario: A JSON input step must read one row per customer from customers.json, which holds an array of customer objects, each with id, name and region_code, under a customers key.
questions.prompt: Which expression on the step's Fields tab reads each customer's region_code?
options: $.region_code[*]
$.customers[*].region_code
region_code
/customers/customer/region_code
questions.explanation: $.customers[*].region_code is a JSONPath that walks every object in the customers array and takes its region_code. /customers/customer/region_code is XPath, the syntax of the XML steps, not JSON. A bare region_code is not a path, so the step cannot locate it. $.region_code[*] looks for an array called region_code at the top level, which does not exist; a wrong path is the usual reason a JSON field comes back empty.

questions.scenario: To add customer fields and then product fields to each sale, you feed the second Stream lookup from the first rather than from the original sales stream.
questions.prompt: Why chain the two lookups this way?
options: A Stream lookup accepts only one incoming hop
The second lookup needs the first one's output sorted
Feeding both from one source would double the rows
Each passes on its row plus what it added, so one row gets both
questions.explanation: A Stream lookup returns the row it received plus the fields it retrieved, so chaining collects the customer fields and then the product fields on one row. Stream lookup takes two inputs, the main stream and the lookup stream, so a single-hop limit is not the reason. Stream lookup needs no sorted input. Feeding both from the sales stream would not double the rows; it would give two streams, each carrying half the enrichment.

questions.scenario: For a customer file you have never seen, you need the number of distinct customer ids and the rows whose id repeats.
questions.prompt: Which steps give you both in one pass?
options: Select values, with the id field marked as unique
Sort rows, then Unique rows with repeats on its error hop
Group by on its own, counting the rows for each id
Filter rows, with a duplicate condition on the id field
questions.explanation: Unique rows compares each row with the one before it, so sorting first brings repeats together; sending the duplicates down its error hop gives the distinct count and the offending rows in the same run. Group by counts rows per id but returns a summary, not the duplicated rows themselves. Filter rows tests each row alone and cannot see repeats. Select values has no uniqueness setting.

questions.scenario: Before designing anything, you want the total amount per category from a new file with a category field and a numeric amount field.
questions.prompt: Which single step gets you there?
options: Merge join, matching category against itself
Text file output, then a pivot in a spreadsheet
Sort rows, ordering the file by category
Group by, grouping on category and summing amount
questions.explanation: Group by does it in one step: name category as the grouping field, sum amount, and preview. Sort rows orders the rows but totals nothing. Writing a file and pivoting in a spreadsheet takes two tools and a manual step. Joining category against itself multiplies rows rather than summarising them.

questions.scenario: A developer who built ten steps and ran them once at the end spends an hour finding a date misparsed at step three.
questions.prompt: Which working habit would have caught the problem at step three?
options: Sorting the rows early so that errors surface first
Running the whole transformation again with detailed logging
Previewing each step as it is added, before adding the next
Adding one validation step just before the output
questions.explanation: Previewing each step as it is added shows the data at the point where an assumption is made, so the misparsed date would have been visible at step three. Detailed logging on a full run still reports the problem at the end, far from its cause. A single validation step before the output detects that something is wrong but not where it went wrong. Sorting does nothing to reveal a misparsed value.

questions.scenario: Before designing a pipeline for a supplier's file, you profile it with a few Group by and Unique rows previews.
questions.prompt: Which findings is profiling most likely to surface?
options: Whether the supplier's system is licensed for production
The character encoding, which PDI cannot detect
The database the file was originally exported from
A stray delimiter, a duplicated key, or two date formats
questions.explanation: Stray delimiters, duplicated keys and mixed date formats are the classic finds, and each quietly breaks a downstream assumption: a column shifts, a join multiplies rows, a sort stops meaning anything. Encoding is set on the input step and is not what profiling a file's contents reveals. Nothing in a file's rows records the database it came from. Licensing is not a property of the data at all.

questions.scenario: One row fails a business rule because its customer id is missing, and another makes a database insert fail outright.
questions.prompt: How does the transformation treat these two rows differently?
options: The rule follows your filter branch; the insert needs error handling
Both rows are caught by the same Filter rows FALSE branch
Neither row is recoverable; the transformation stops on either
Both rows go down the output step's error hop automatically
questions.explanation: A business rule is your own logic, so the failing row goes down whichever Filter rows branch you designed; a failed insert is a technical error inside a step and stops the transformation unless you enable error handling on that step. The FALSE branch only sees rows that reach the filter, not failures inside a later step. Nothing goes to an error hop automatically; it must be switched on. The rule failure is fully recoverable, because it is just a branch.

questions.scenario: A colleague plans to enrich an order stream against a 40-million-row reference table, using a Stream lookup.
questions.prompt: What is the problem with that plan?
options: Stream lookup cannot read from a database, only from a file
Stream lookup returns every match, so the row count would explode
Stream lookup needs both streams sorted, and that table is not
Stream lookup holds the whole reference set in memory, and it will not fit
questions.explanation: Stream lookup gets its speed by loading the whole lookup stream into memory, which is right for a small code table and wrong for 40 million rows; a Database lookup or a Merge join suits that size. Stream lookup can take its lookup rows from any step, including a database input. It needs no sorted input. It returns at most one match per row, so rows cannot multiply.
